analysis.one_liner: Lets financial firms petition federal regulators to waive rules covering their new products.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with no cosponsors in the last three weeks of the 117th Congress, was referred to two House committees and died without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let any company offering a technology-enabled financial product petition nine federal regulators — including the Federal Reserve, the SEC, and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau — to modify or waive the rules that apply to it. While a petition was pending, regulators could not take enforcement action against the firm, and if a petition was approved, other agencies and state regulators would generally be barred from enforcing their own rules against that product. Each agency would also stand up a new 'Financial Services Innovation Office' to help firms through the process.
analysis.who_benefits: Financial firms — from fintech startups to crypto platforms to large banks — that want to launch products under lighter rules. They would get a government office to help them navigate regulators, a listed menu of rules agencies are willing to waive, immunity from enforcement while their petition is pending, and, if approved, a binding agreement that blocks other federal agencies and states from stepping in. They could also choose arbitration instead of court challenges.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires each of nine financial agencies to publish a list of at least three regulatory areas it would consider modifying or waiving through the petition process, giving firms a clear menu of rules up for relaxation.

A firm could petition to modify or waive not just agency regulations but federal statutory requirements, and the agency must grant the waiver if it finds a 'rational basis' that the rule is 'unduly burdensome' to the firm.

From the moment a firm files a petition, regulators are barred from taking enforcement action against that product; the only check is that an agency can ask a court for an injunction if it finds immediate danger to consumers or systemic risk.

Once a firm signs an 'enforceable compliance agreement,' other federal agencies may not bring enforcement actions against the product, and states may not either unless a court finds the federal agency's approval was arbitrary and the product substantially harmed consumers in that state.

Each agency must create a Financial Services Innovation Office whose duties include helping approved firms comply, defending waivers against challenges, and reducing the 'time and cost' of offering new products.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers and investors, who would bear whatever risk comes from firms operating under waived rules — with weaker backstops, since state enforcers like state attorneys general would generally be locked out and petition data could be kept confidential. The nine agencies would also split the cost of running the new offices from 2023 through 2027.

drawbacks.text: The enforcement safe harbor means a firm can begin or continue offering a product with no regulator able to act against it while the petition is pending — only a court injunction for 'immediate danger' or systemic risk stands in the way.

The bill would preempt state enforcement: after an agreement is signed, states cannot act against the product unless a court first rules that the federal agency acted arbitrarily and that the product substantially harmed consumers — a high bar that shifts policing away from the enforcers closest to consumers.

The bill lets agencies keep petition data confidential and lets firms elect arbitration instead of court proceedings, reducing public visibility into which rules were waived and how products behave afterward.

Agencies must approve a petition if the firm shows it is 'more likely than not' that its alternative compliance plan serves the public interest and improves access — a company-friendly standard, and a firm whose petition is denied can simply revise and resubmit within 90 days.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated purpose — cutting red tape so new financial products reach consumers faster — is a real goal, and a structured petition process is less arbitrary than ad-hoc waivers. But the design goes far beyond a sandbox: it allows waiver of statutes themselves, immunizes firms from enforcement while petitions are pending, locks state enforcers out after approval, and keeps the terms confidential. For ordinary people, the loss of enforcement leverage and transparency outweighs the promise of faster product launches, especially since regulators already have tools like no-action letters to handle novel products case by case.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced with zero cosponsors in the final weeks of the 117th Congress, the bill was sent to the Financial Services and Agriculture committees, neither of which took it up before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Patrick McHenry, the top Republican on the House Financial Services Committee, introduced the Financial Services Innovation Act of 2022 on December 14, 2022.
No other member cosponsored the bill.
It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and, for relevant provisions, to the House Agriculture Committee; no hearing, markup, or floor action followed.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and all bills not passed expire with it, so the bill died in committee without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, no firm gained waiver rights or enforcement immunity, and federal and state regulators kept their existing authority over financial products. Consumers keep current protections; the fintech and financial firms the bill was written for get nothing from it. Had it been reintroduced later, its champion went on to chair the Financial Services Committee in the next Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Regulators and consumers kept the status quo

for.name: Rep. Patrick McHenry

against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended.

against.what_they_did: Took no action on the provisions within its jurisdiction before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so the partisan shape was never tested; the bill was a Republican leadership-backed idea that attracted no members of either party in its three-week life.

industries.industry: Fintech, crypto, and technology-enabled financial firms
industries.note: The bill hands these firms a formal channel to have consumer-protection and other financial rules waived, plus immunity from enforcement while petitions are pending and protection from state enforcers afterward. Some innovations do expand access to banking and credit, but the mechanism is built to remove regulatory friction for firms, and the cost of loosened oversight falls on the customers using the products.

Any company — including established banks — can file petitions, so incumbents could use the process to shed rules, and firms 'similarly situated' to an approved petitioner can skip the public comment period entirely. That fast-track makes the waiver process cheaper for the biggest players.

industries.industry: State financial regulators and state enforcers
industries.note: Once a federal agency signs an agreement with a firm, states are barred from enforcing their own laws against that product unless a court finds the federal approval was arbitrary and consumers were substantially harmed. State regulators, who often act faster and closer to consumers than federal agencies, would lose their main leverage.

industries.industry: Federal financial regulators (Fed, SEC, CFPB, CFTC, FDIC, OCC, Treasury, FHFA, NCUA)
industries.note: The bill would obligate each agency to create an innovation office charged with promoting financial products and helping firms win waivers, and agencies would bear the cost of the program. Their discretionary enforcement authority over petitioning firms would be sharply limited.
